title: Amyraut distinguishes motions of the will that follow deliberation from those that do not
source_text: XIV. Similis est hac in parte Doctrina Mosis Amyraldi nuper in Academia Salmuriensi Professoris Tractatu de libero hominis arbitrio, p. 61. & seqq. Ubi primo distinguit duplicem voluntatis motionem. Unam quae non est sejuncta quidem ab ea cognitione quae a ratione ducit originem, sed est istiusmodi tamen ut cognitio ex qua nascitur ac efflorescit, non sit ipsa orta ex praevia consultatione: alteram quae non modo conjuncta est cum aliqua cognitione, sed nascitur ex ea notitia quam προβούλευσις, i. e. consultatio antecessit, & quae nihil aliud est quam Conclusio quae ex deliberatione conficitur, consideratis, scilicet, atque comparatis inter se pluribus objectis, aut uno & eodem objecto spectato diversimode, adeo ut mens aliquandiu hinc & illinc rationum librata ponderibus, tandem in unam partem inclinetur. Deinde observat illam voluntatis motionem, quae nullam mentis consultationem & deliberationem sequitur, adhuc duplicem esse, nimirum voluntatem per unam in finem, id est, beatitudinem & felicitatem ipsam ferri; per alteram in media quae ad finem istum ducere existimantur.
pass_a_gloss: Similar in this part is the Doctrine of Moses Amyraut lately Professor in the Academy of Saumur in the Treatise on the free choice of man, p. 61. & following. Where first he distinguishes a twofold motion of the will. One which is not indeed separated from that knowledge which draws its origin from reason, but is yet of such a kind that the knowledge from which it is born and blossoms, has not itself arisen from previous consultation: the other which not only is joined with some knowledge, but is born from that knowledge which probouleusis, i.e. consultation preceded, & which is nothing else than the Conclusion which is made from deliberation, several objects, namely, being considered and compared among themselves, or one & the same object viewed in different ways, so that the mind balanced for some while hither & thither by the weights of reasons, at length inclines to one side. Then he observes that that motion of the will, which follows no consultation and deliberation of the mind, is again twofold, namely that by one the will is carried to the end, that is, to blessedness and happiness itself; by the other to the means which are thought to lead to that end.
pass_b_english: Moses Amyraut, until recently professor at the Academy of Saumur, teaches much the same on this point in his treatise On Man's Free Choice (p. 61 and following). He first distinguishes two movements of the will.

One is not cut off from the knowledge that has its source in reason, but the knowledge from which it springs and grows did not itself come out of any prior weighing. The other is not only joined with knowledge but arises from knowledge that consultation (probouleusis) went before. That knowledge is simply the conclusion reached by deliberation, when several objects are considered and compared, or one and the same object is looked at in different ways, so that the mind, swung this way and that for a while by the weight of reasons, finally leans to one side.

Next he observes that the movement of the will that follows no weighing or deliberation by the mind is itself of two kinds. By one the will is carried toward the end, namely happiness and blessedness itself; by the other toward the means thought to lead to that end.

choices.why: The image is of a plant flowering from its root; 'springs and grows' keeps the organic metaphor without strain.
